problem: Multi-robot exploration/search coordination relies on geometric objectives (frontiers, information gain, Voronoi/CVRP) and cannot use semantic priors or task intent. Existing LLM/VLM multi-robot coordinators feed raw images or dense maps, causing large prompts and high latency.
motivation: Search tasks like 'find my jacket in the bedroom' need room-level semantic reasoning beyond coverage. A compact structured abstraction could let an LLM reason about semantics and topology in near real time while classical planners handle geometry.
key_idea: Compress the semantic occupancy map into a room-level semantic area graph that an LLM uses to assign robots to rooms, with deterministic frontier planning and local navigation executing inside the assigned rooms.
insight: Structured text abstraction gives task-aware coordination with under 500 tokens per query (~2.5 s). The gain is on semantic search, not pure exploration, and grows with environment size (large: ~19% faster than Hungarian). Ablations show that the target room type (+16.0% time when removed), plan summary (+13.0%) and neighborhood connectivity (+9.6%) each matter.
method: Frontier detection: classical Yamauchi frontiers (free cell adjacent to unknown, 4-connected), BFS clustering with max distance c_max; each cluster has a centroid waypoint projected to the nearest free cell, and a size.

Semantic area graph: nodes are connected components of free cells with the same room label (room instances); edges join rooms with 4-adjacent free cells; nodes store room type, frontier clusters, robots and neighbours; rooms with no frontiers are pruned; rebuilt every coordination cycle.

LLM room-level planning: the serialized graph, previous plan summary, task spec and target room type go to the LLM every T_coord=50 steps. It outputs a plan summary and a mapping from each robot to exactly one room id. Exploration favours rooms with many frontiers; search favours rooms matching the target type while keeping robots spatially diverse.
Frontier selection: within a room, frontier clusters are allocated to the robots assigned there by iterative Hungarian matching on Euclidean distance, then ordered per robot with a TSP solver.

Local execution: robots visit their frontier waypoints sequentially with motion planning on the observed map, and fall back to the nearest reachable frontier if the list is exhausted or a path is infeasible.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen, temperature 0.2, max 1000 tokens); ablations with Claude-Haiku-4.5, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B
setting.observation: Onboard camera per robot giving a partially observable semantic occupancy grid (occupancy plus room-type labels from a scene recognition model, treated as upstream input)
setting.action_space: Frontier waypoints executed by a motion planner on the grid map (2-4 robots, planar pose)
setting.simulator: Habitat-Matterport3D (HM3D) apartment scenes, custom multi-robot setup
setting.privileged: Room-type semantic labels supplied by an upstream perception module (semantic room map); target room type given as prior

results: SAGR is best on semantic search at every scale; in large environments it cuts search time about 19.2% vs Hungarian (282.1 to 228.0) and 18.8% vs AEP+DVC (280.8 to 228.0). On pure exploration it stays competitive but is slightly worse than the best geometric baseline (e.g. 825.6 vs 738.6 for AEP+DVC on large). Each query takes about 2.5 s with under 500 tokens.
limitations: Evaluation is only in simulation, on 10 HM3D layouts with at most 4 robots, no real robots, and no comparison with LLM-based multi-robot methods like CoNavGPT or COMRES-VLM.

Relies on an upstream perception module for accurate room labels and on the target's room type being known in advance; the LLM adds stochasticity and about 2.5 s latency, and the gains are not large on small maps.
Search-time variance is high (std about 140-180 steps), and no significance tests are reported.
